common_name: H-63A American Persimmon (Claypool Caramel-Flavored Native Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; H-63A grows in a distinctly upright, narrow habit and benefits from a second American persimmon cultivar planted nearby to improve fruit set.

directions: H-63A is a named selection from the late James Claypool's extensive Indiana persimmon breeding program, distributed today mainly through collector nurseries and Northern Nut Growers Association members. It is prized among American persimmon enthusiasts for a distinctive rum- and caramelized-sugar-like flavor note layered over the typical rich, honeyed sweetness of a fully ripe native persimmon, making it a favorite for puddings, pies, and fruit leather. Fruit is medium-sized and deep orange, and like all Diospyros virginiana selections it remains firm and strongly astringent until fully soft-ripened by cool fall weather, after which the flesh turns custardy and sweet. The tree has a notably upright, narrow growth habit compared to many seedling persimmons, which can make it easier to site in smaller home orchards. It tolerates heat, drought, and a range of soils once established, and benefits from thinning of root suckers to prevent thicket formation.

common_name: NC-10 American Persimmon (Campbell NC10, Cold-Hardy Seedless Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; NC-10 is female and sets seedless fruit without a pollinator, though it tolerates cold winters well for the species.

directions: NC-10, also sold as Campbell NC10, arose as a seedling of the classic Early Golden cultivar selected in Ontario's Niagara region and has since been distributed by cold-climate specialty nurseries as one of the hardier named American persimmon selections. It bears medium-sized, oval fruit, seedless when grown without a male pollinator nearby, that ripens over a long window from mid-September through late October. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections the fruit is firmly astringent until fully soft, at which point it develops a very sweet, rich flavor and pudding-like texture. NC-10 is valued particularly by growers at the northern edge of American persimmon's range for its reliable ripening and good winter hardiness. Site trees in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, and avoid disturbing the taproot when transplanting.

common_name: Lena American Persimmon (Large Low-Astringency Claypool-Program Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Lena ripens late in the season, so site it where fall frosts arrive as late as possible to allow fruit to fully soften on the tree.

directions: Lena, also recorded as L-104, is a named selection from James Claypool's Indiana American persimmon breeding program and has been propagated and passed along through collector orchards, including Jerry Lehman's persimmon research farm in Terre Haute, Indiana. It produces large fruit for the species with red-orange flesh, and it is noted among American persimmon growers for being especially low in astringency even before fruit is fully soft, though as with all Diospyros virginiana selections the best flavor and sweetness develop only after full ripening. Lena ripens late in the fall relative to earlier cultivars such as Early Golden, so it suits growers with a longer autumn season. The tree shares the general toughness of native persimmon, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soils once established, and needs little maintenance beyond removing root suckers.

common_name: Woolbright American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Early-Ripening Native Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Woolbright fruit softens and splits readily once ripe, so harvest daily from the ground during the early October ripening window to avoid loss to wildlife and rot.

directions: Woolbright is a long-documented named selection of American persimmon, cataloged alongside classic cultivars such as Early Golden, John Rick, and Miller in pomological surveys of the species. It produces large fruit, typically carrying two to eight seeds, with excellent rich, sweet flavor once fully ripe. Fruit ripens comparatively early, around the start of October, but the flesh is notably soft and splits easily once it falls, so it is best gathered promptly rather than left to accumulate on the ground. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections, unripe fruit is strongly astringent and must be allowed to fully soften before eating. Woolbright is a productive, reliable bearer and tolerates the heat, drought, and marginal soils typical of native persimmon growing conditions once established.
